hypoxia.short: Too little oxygen reaching the body's tissues. At altitude it starts because the air you breathe has a lower oxygen pressure.

barometric-pressure.short: The pressure of the air around you, from the weight of the air above. It is about 760 mmHg at sea level and falls as you climb.

fio2.short: The fraction of the air you breathe that is oxygen: 0.209 (20.9%) at every altitude on Earth, and lower only in a tent or mask that removes oxygen.

pio2.short: The oxygen pressure in the air once it has reached your airways and is full of water vapour: FiO₂ × (PB − 47 mmHg). About 150 mmHg at sea level.

hypobaric-hypoxia.short: Low oxygen because the air pressure is low (real altitude, or a chamber that lowers the pressure). The oxygen share of the air stays 20.9%.

normobaric-hypoxia.short: Low oxygen at normal air pressure, made by taking oxygen out of the air (a tent, room or mask). The oxygen share is lower, for example 15%.

altitude-acclimatisation.short: The body's adjustments to a lower oxygen pressure over hours to weeks: more breathing, a smaller plasma volume, then more red cells.

hypoxic-ventilatory-response.short: The rise in breathing when oxygen pressure falls, driven by sensors in the neck arteries. It starts within minutes and grows over days.

respiratory-alkalosis.short: Blood that is too alkaline because extra breathing blows off CO₂. At altitude it is the price of breathing more; the kidneys correct it over days.

acute-mountain-sickness.short: Headache with nausea, loss of appetite, poor sleep or dizziness in the first day or two at altitude. Usually mild and temporary; worse symptoms need descent.

hape.short: Fluid in the lungs at altitude: breathlessness at rest, cough, weakness. Rare below 3,000 m. A medical emergency that needs descent.

hace.short: Swelling of the brain at altitude: confusion, unsteady walking, severe headache. Not seen below about 4,000 m. A medical emergency that needs descent.

live-high-train-high.short: The classic altitude camp: you sleep and train at altitude, usually 2,000–2,500 m, for weeks.

intermittent-hypoxic-exposure.short: Short spells of breathing low-oxygen air at rest (for example 1 hour a day), living and training at sea level.

intermittent-hypoxic-training.short: Doing some training sessions in low-oxygen air (a chamber or mask) while living at or near sea level.

repeated-sprint-training-in-hypoxia.short: Several short all-out sprints (under 30 s) with short rests, done in low-oxygen air; a team-sport version of hypoxic training.

hypoxic-dose.short: How much hypoxia you took in: altitude and time together. One common unit is kilometre-hours (km·h): altitude in km × total hours of exposure.

neocytolysis.short: The fast breakdown of the youngest red cells after you come down from altitude, when EPO falls. It may shrink the gain in red cells within weeks.

prediction-interval.short: The range in which a single new person's result is expected to fall (here 95% of the time). It is wider than a confidence interval for the average.

pre-acclimatisation.short: Getting used to altitude before you travel, for example by sleeping in a low-oxygen tent at home for 1–3 weeks.
